summary: Discusses what it means to be on the Internet and gives terminology to distinguish levels of access for service consumers and providers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines four terms for different ways users and organizations access Internet services. The categories range from a permanent TCP/IP connection to access limited to email and network news.

questions: what does on the internet mean
what does it mean to be on the internet
subtitle: Four terms for different levels of user and provider Internet access.

tldr.problem: The phrase “on the Internet” can describe different levels of access with different capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: The memo distinguishes Full, Client, Mediated, and Messaging access from the user's perspective, ordered from most to least access.
tldr.outcome: The terms give users and providers a vocabulary for describing basic types of Internet attachment; the memo does not define security mechanisms.

today: RFC 1775 is Informational. It proposes terminology for distinguishing levels of user and provider access to Internet services.

sections.title: Why Distinguish Access Levels
sections.content:
The memo says Internet growth created confusion about whether a user or organization was “on” the Internet. It offers user-focused terms to distinguish access capabilities, based mainly on the application services a user can use.

The four categories are ordered from most to least access and distinguish providers from consumers of Internet services.
sections.plainLanguage: People can use Internet services in different ways, so a single phrase may not describe what they can do. The RFC proposes four categories to make those differences clearer.

sections.title: The Four Access Categories
sections.content:
Full Access is a permanent, full-time TCP/IP attachment, mainly associated with service providers and machines that are directly visible to others. Client Access means a user runs Internet applications on their own computer, though the connection may be intermittent or constrained.

Mediated Access means a provider runs Internet applications on its own computer for the user; the user's platform is not directly on the Internet. Messaging Access provides access only through electronic mail and network news, which can carry information with high latency but are not interactive.
sections.plainLanguage: Full access connects a system continuously. Client access runs Internet applications on the user's computer; mediated access runs them through a provider; messaging access is limited to email and news.

sections.title: Examples of Access Types
sections.content:
The memo classifies a home user who dials into a public service and runs applications on the provider's system as having Mediated access. A user connecting by SLIP or PPP and running applications on their own computer has Client access.

A corporation with a full-time TCP/IP connection has Full access. An employee running applications through a firewall has Client access, while an employee who must connect to a special machine that runs those applications has Mediated access.
sections.plainLanguage: Access type depends on where the Internet applications run. A dial-up terminal to a provider is mediated; running applications on one's own computer is client access.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC does not define security mechanisms. It cautions readers to consider the different security implications of the access scenarios when choosing a service.
sections.plainLanguage: The categories do not provide security protections. The memo advises readers to consider the security implications of each service.
